flashcards.q: What are the four git object types and what does each contain?
flashcards.a: blob (raw file content, no name/path), tree (mode+name+type+sha rows pointing to blobs/trees), commit (tree sha, parent sha(s), author/committer, message), tag (named/signed pointer to any object).

flashcards.q: What is a git branch, physically?
flashcards.a: A 41-byte (40 hex + newline) file under .git/refs/heads/<name> holding a single commit SHA. Moving a branch is just overwriting that file.

flashcards.q: Why do rebased commits get new SHAs even if the diff content is identical?
flashcards.a: A commit's hash covers tree sha + parent sha(s) + author/committer + message. Rebase changes the parent, so the hash changes even when the resulting file tree is byte-identical.

flashcards.q: What is git reflog's default retention window?
flashcards.a: 90 days for entries reachable from a ref, 30 days for entries that become unreachable (gc.reflogExpire / gc.reflogExpireUnreachable). After that + an actual git gc --prune, objects become eligible for real deletion.

flashcards.q: How do you recover work after a bad `git reset --hard`?
flashcards.a: git reflog to find the SHA the branch pointed to before the reset, then git branch <name> <sha> to re-point a branch at it. Objects aren't actually deleted until gc prunes unreachable ones.

flashcards.q: What does `--force-with-lease` check that plain `--force` doesn't?
flashcards.a: It refuses the push if the remote-tracking ref (your local cached view of origin/<branch>) doesn't match the remote's actual current ref -- meaning someone else pushed since your last fetch. Plain --force overwrites unconditionally.

flashcards.q: What is the complexity of git bisect and why?
flashcards.a: O(log2 N) checkouts for N commits in range -- it's a binary search over a linear history, halving the remaining range each step.

flashcards.q: What do the exit codes mean in `git bisect run <script>`?
flashcards.a: 0 = good, 1-127 (except 125) = bad, 125 = skip (commit is untestable, e.g. doesn't build).

flashcards.q: What is the constraint on git worktrees regarding branches?
flashcards.a: All worktrees share the same object database and refs, so the same branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees simultaneously -- git refuses since both would try to move the same ref independently.

flashcards.q: Is the reflog shared with remote collaborators?
flashcards.a: No. The reflog is local-only, lives under .git/logs, was never pushed, and does not exist for anyone else's clone -- it can't recover a commit you never had locally.

flashcards.q: What tool finds dangling (unreachable, not-yet-pruned) commits when the reflog doesn't have the answer?
flashcards.a: git fsck --lost-found -- lists dangling objects not reachable from any ref, writing loose ones to .git/lost-found/commit/<sha>.
Surgically replays only the commits in the range (oldbase..branch] onto <newbase>, without dragging along unrelated commits before oldbase.
